summary: Describes how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) to authenticate peers in IKE and IKEv2. ECDSA can offer faster computation, smaller signatures and lower bandwidth use.

eli5.summary: To prove a letter is from you, you sign it. ECDSA is a signing method that uses a small, clever kind of math, so the signature is short and quick to check when two computers set up a secure link.

subtitle: Adds elliptic curve signatures as a third way for IPsec peers to prove who they are during IKE and IKEv2.

tldr.problem: IKE and IKEv2 only offered RSA and DSA signatures for peer authentication, and ECDSA could give smaller signatures and faster computation at comparable strength.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three signature algorithms, ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521, each fixing an elliptic curve group and a SHA hash, and says the signature is sent as the concatenation of two integers r and s.
tldr.outcome: ECDSA authentication is added without changing how IKE otherwise works. It is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 4754 is a Proposed Standard from January 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 4753 for the curve groups.

sections.title: Why Add Another Signature Method
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) is a key agreement and security negotiation protocol used to establish keys for IPsec. Early in the exchange, both parties must authenticate each other using a negotiated method. In the original IKE this happens in Phase 1. In IKEv2 it happens in the exchange called IKE-AUTH.

One authentication option is a digital signature made with public key cryptography. Before this RFC, two signature methods were defined for Phase 1 and IKE-AUTH: RSA signatures and Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) signatures. RFC 4754 introduces ECDSA signatures as a third method.

The RFC argues that for any given level of security against the best known attacks, ECDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures and ECDSA keys need less bandwidth than DSA keys. It also points to speed and efficiency advantages in many settings. It adds that using elliptic curve groups for the IKE key exchange as well can add more efficiency. The abstract stresses that no changes to existing IKE operation are introduced.
sections.eli5: Two computers that want to talk privately first have to show each other ID. Until now they could use two kinds of ID card. This RFC adds a third kind that is smaller and faster to check.

sections.title: What ECDSA Is
sections.content:
The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is the elliptic curve analogue of the DSA (DSS) signature method. It is defined in the ANSI X9.62 standard. The RFC lists other compatible specifications: FIPS 186-2, IEEE 1363, IEEE 1363A and SEC1.

The claimed benefits are practical. ECDSA signatures are smaller than RSA signatures of similar cryptographic strength. ECDSA public keys and certificates are smaller than DSA keys of similar strength, which improves communications efficiency. On many platforms ECDSA operations can also be computed more quickly than similar-strength RSA or DSA operations.
sections.eli5: ECDSA is a signing trick based on curvy math. For the same level of safety, the signature is shorter than with older tricks, so it is cheaper to send and often quicker to check.

sections.title: Three Algorithms, Each With a Curve and a Hash
sections.content:
The original IKE has two phases, and in Phase 1 the parties authenticate with pre-shared keys, digital signatures or public key encryption. IKEv2 starts with two exchanges, IKE-SA-INIT and IKE-AUTH. When extensible authentication is not used, IKE-AUTH includes a digital signature or a Message Authentication Code (MAC) on a block of data.

The IANA-assigned attribute number for generic ECDSA in IKE is 8, but the IKEv2 list of authentication methods did not include ECDSA. IKEv2 also has no transform type for hash functions, so ECDSA cannot be named separately from its hash. For that reason the hash function has to be part of the signature algorithm, and the elliptic curve group has to be specified because the hash choice depends on it.

The result is three signature algorithms, ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521. Each one is ECDSA instantiated with a particular curve group and hash. For consistency, the RFC defines the signatures for IKE the same way. The curve groups and base points come from RFC 4753. In the IANA section, IANA updated its IKE and IKEv2 authentication method registries to include the three algorithms.

The algorithm name matches the curve size, except ECDSA-521, which pairs a 521-bit group with SHA-512.
sections.eli5: Because the system cannot pick a signing method and a scrambler separately, the RFC sells them as three ready-made kits: small, medium and large. Each kit already has its curve and scrambler chosen.

sections.title: How the Signature Is Encoded
sections.content:
When any of the three algorithms is used in IKE or IKEv2, the signature payload SHALL contain the computed signature as the concatenation of a pair of integers r and s. The RFC fixes the width of each integer so the payload has a predictable size.

If a value is shorter than its required width, it is padded by pre-pending zeros. Note that ECDSA-521 uses 528-bit integers, not 521, so the padding applies there.
sections.eli5: The signature is two numbers written side by side. Each number is always written with the same number of digits, and if a number is short, zeros are added at the front, like writing 007 instead of 7.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
Most of the RFC is test vectors, one set per algorithm, so implementers can check their code. Each example signs the message abc (hex 616263) and shows the curve parameters, the static and ephemeral keys, the hash, the signature and the intermediate values needed to verify it. IANA assigned the ID values 9 to ECDSA-256, 10 to ECDSA-384 and 11 to ECDSA-521.

The signer computes r as the first coordinate of the ephemeral public key reduced modulo the group order q, and s as (h + r*w) * kinv modulo q. The verifier computes sinv, then u = h*sinv and v = r*sinv, adds the points (gx,gy)^u and (gwx,gwy)^v, and accepts the signature if the x coordinate of the sum, reduced modulo q, equals r. Each vector ends with an example of what the IKEv2 authentication payload would look like.
sections.eli5: These are worked examples with the answers shown, like a math textbook with the solutions at the back. If your program gets the same answers, it is probably doing the signing right.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the document proposes new digital signatures for IKE and IKEv2, many security considerations from the IKE and IKEv2 specifications apply here as well. Implementers should make sure appropriate security measures are in place when they deploy ECDSA within IKE or IKEv2.

The RFC states that ECDSA-256, ECDSA-384 and ECDSA-521 are designed to offer security comparable with AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256 respectively.
sections.eli5: The big, medium and small kits are built to be about as hard to break as three different strengths of another well known lock. You still have to install them carefully.
